Choosing the right translation service provider for you

May 8, 2017
Translation agency | Translation companies | Translation services

Choosing a translation service provider is easier when you know who does what. The market runs from individual freelancers to global language companies, and each model suits a different type of project.

Here is how the main types of translation provider differ, what to ask before you hire one and how to match the provider to your content.

Freelance translators

Many translators work for themselves. You will meet three versions of the freelance model.

A freelance translator who takes your project directly

You contact the translator, send your documents and agree the brief. This suits a single language pair and a clearly defined subject.

Bear in mind that a freelancer works alone. If your deadline moves, your volume grows or you need a second language, the capacity may not be there.

A freelance translator who subcontracts to colleagues

Some freelancers pass overflow work to trusted colleagues and keep a commission. They usually review the colleague's work before they send you the final version.

Ask who is actually translating your text and who checks it. You are entitled to a straight answer.

A freelance project manager

A freelance project manager does not translate. They hold a list of translators across subjects and language combinations and coordinate the work for you.

This can work well for multilingual projects, provided the project manager can show you who the translators are and how they are vetted.

Translation agencies

A translation agency can take your project from first brief to final delivery. Agencies differ widely in size and in the way they operate.

Small agencies

Two or three people, often former colleagues from the same specialism, run the business and usually translate themselves. You get direct contact with the people doing the work, but the range of languages is narrower.

Translator networks

In a network, several professional translators pool their knowledge and experience under one brand. This is the model behind BeTranslated.

Members still produce their own translations, and every text is proofread by a second linguist before it reaches you. You get the breadth of an agency with the accountability of a small team.

Medium-sized agencies

These agencies employ project managers and specialists in desktop publishing, web formats and localisation. Everyone has a defined role, and independent translators are usually briefed on each project.

This model suits businesses with a steady flow of work in several languages.

Large agencies and global language companies

Large providers operate from several offices and manage hundreds of projects at once. They can cover almost any language and subject, and they offer scale, technology and formal processes.

The trade-off is distance. You may deal with an account manager rather than the linguist, and a small project can compete for attention with very large accounts.

How to choose a translation service provider

Once you know the type of provider that fits, test the shortlist against five practical points.

Match the language and the region

Be precise about your target audience. Spanish for Madrid is not Spanish for Mexico City, and French for Brussels is not identical to French for Montreal.

Ask which linguists will handle your language combination and whether they live in, or know well, the market you are targeting.

Look for subject expertise

A good linguist is not enough on its own. A contract needs a legal translator, a user manual needs a technical translator and a campaign needs a translator who can write persuasively.

Ask for examples of similar work, or the profiles of the translators who would take on your project. A provider that specialises in your sector will make fewer terminology mistakes.

Check the quality process

Ask whether a second qualified linguist reviews every translation. The international standard for translation services, ISO 17100, requires translation by a qualified translator and revision by a second person, so a provider that works to it should be able to describe that step.

Ask too about confidentiality, how files are stored and what happens if you spot an error after delivery.

Read reviews with a critical eye

Look at reviews, case studies and the client list. Decide first what matters to you: speed, specialist knowledge or a named contact who answers quickly.

Then check whether the clients mentioned resemble your business. Praise from a consumer brand tells you little if you need a legal translator.

Request a short sample

Many providers will translate a short passage, often around 300 words, so you can judge quality before you commit. Do not expect pages of free work, especially on a small project.

If you cannot read the target language, ask a colleague or customer in that country to review the sample.

Which type of provider suits which project

A one-off letter in a single language pair may suit a freelancer. A recurring flow of marketing, legal and technical content in several languages usually calls for an agency or a network.

If your document must be accepted by a UK authority, check the rules first. Home Office guidance for visa applications asks for a translator's confirmation that the translation is accurate, the date, the translator's full name and signature and their contact details. Your provider should offer a certified translation with those details as standard.

Ask for the same clarity on any extras you need, such as proofreading, desktop publishing, localisation or interpreting.

Next steps

List your languages, subject areas, volumes and deadlines before you contact anyone. A clear brief makes quotes comparable and avoids surprises on price.

If you would like to talk it through, request a free, no-obligation quote from BeTranslated. You can also read about our clients before you decide.

Frequently asked questions

What is a translation service provider?

A translation service provider is any person or company that translates text for clients. It can be a freelancer, a small agency, a translator network or a large language company. The right choice depends on the languages, subject and volume of your project.

Should I use a freelancer or a translation agency?

A freelancer suits a small project in one language pair. An agency or network suits several languages, tight deadlines or content that needs a second linguist to check it. Ask either option who reviews the final text.

How do I know a translation provider is any good?

Ask about the translators' qualifications and subject experience, the review process and past work in your sector. A short paid or free sample also helps. Reviews and named clients give useful context but should not replace those checks.

Do I need a certified translation in the UK?

You need one when an authority asks for it, for example the Home Office for a visa application or a UK court. A certified translation includes the translator's signed confirmation of accuracy, the date and their contact details. Check the requirements of the body that will receive the document before you order.

How much does a translation service provider charge?

Prices depend on the language pair, subject, length and any extras such as certification or desktop publishing. Providers usually quote per word or per project. Send your document for a quote and compare what each price includes, not only the total.
